# RootGuard: IoT Soil Moisture Monitor {.section-title}
**Context:** Personal Project · ESP32-C5, Electronics & Autodesk Inventor

A battery-powered soil monitor built to stop me from overwatering my Monstera, used as a hands-on project to learn 3D CAD design, soldering, and low-power microcontroller programming.

---

### Why I Built It
* **The Plant Problem:** I kept overwatering my *Monstera deliciosa*. The top couple of centimeters of soil would look dry, but the root zone underneath was still completely saturated.
* **The Excuse to Build:** Instead of buying an off-the-shelf plastic moisture meter, I decided to make my own. It gave me a practical reason to get comfortable with CAD modeling in Autodesk Inventor, schematic reading, soldering rework, and embedded C++.

---

### The Build
* **The Hardware:** Built around a DFRobot FireBeetle 2 ESP32-C5 board, a 0.96" I2C OLED screen, a small 500 mAh LiPo battery, and a capacitive soil probe (which measures soil capacitance rather than running current through the dirt, so it does not corrode like cheap resistive sensors).
* **The 3D-Printed Case:** Modeled a custom enclosure in Autodesk Inventor with mounting bosses for the board, a slot for the battery, and a cutout for the screen. Leaving small 0.25 mm clearances meant everything snapped and screwed together cleanly on the first print.
* **How It Operates:** The station sleeps most of the time to save battery. A quick tap of the button wakes the screen for 5 seconds to show current moisture, a trend arrow, and the battery level. Holding the button starts a temporary Wi-Fi hotspot so I can open a dashboard on my phone to view past readings or calibrate the sensor.

---

### Hardware Bugs & Learning to Solder
Getting the prototype to run reliably was the most interesting part of the project. The first version suffered from erratic wakeups, floating readings, and a battery that died within two days.

Tracing the FireBeetle schematic and pinout definitions revealed a few real-world issues:

* **Wrong Wakeup Pin:** The button was originally wired to a pin that sat outside the chip's low-power wakeup domain.
* **The Sneaky Status LED:** The sensor ground switch was shared with the board's built-in green LED. Turning off the sensor accidentally lit the LED, secretly pulling 2-3 mA around the clock.

To fix it, I learned how to solder and rework the board myself:
* Desoldered and moved the button to a proper low-power wakeup pin (`GPIO 6`).
* Changed the sensor pin mode in code to high-impedance (`Hi-Z`) during sleep so both the probe and the green LED shut off completely, dropping sleep current down to microamps.

---

### Key Takeaways
* **Always check the schematic first:** Reading pin routing and shared lines before wiring saves hours of debugging down the line.
* **Low-power is tricky:** A single floating pin or an unaddressed status LED can quietly destroy battery life.
* **Designing for 3D printing:** Measuring real component tolerances before modeling makes a huge difference between a messy fit and a clean first print.
